meta.titre: Ecosystems: Trophic Levels, Energy Flow and Ecological Pyramids
meta.sous_theme: Structure and energy flow in ecosystems

sections.contenu_markdown: On the Adamawa plateau, cattle graze on grass that has been growing in the rains, and a hawk circles above the pasture looking for a grasshopper or a small lizard. Every farmer and fisherman in Cameroon depends on how energy and nutrients move through such living communities. The GCE Advanced Level paper regularly asks you to name trophic levels, explain why food chains are short, draw or interpret pyramids and describe how the physical conditions in soil decide which organisms live where. This lesson sets out the vocabulary and the calculations that you need.

items: Photosynthesis uses light energy to make organic compounds from carbon dioxide and water.
Respiration releases energy from organic compounds, and some of this energy is lost as heat.
A habitat is the place where an organism lives and a population is a group of organisms of one species in an area.
Bacteria and fungi decompose dead organisms and release nutrients.

sections.titre: Ecosystem structure, trophic levels, energy flow and pyramids
sections.contenu_markdown:
An **ecosystem** is a community of living organisms (the **biotic** component) together with the non-living (**abiotic**) physical and chemical factors of their environment, interacting as a unit. A **community** is all the populations of different species living in the same place at the same time.

**Trophic levels.** A trophic level is the feeding position of an organism in a food chain. Arrows point from the organism that is eaten to the organism that eats it, because they show the direction of energy flow.

| Trophic level | Role | Example in a savanna |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Producer (autotroph) | grass |
| 2 | Primary consumer (herbivore) | goat, grasshopper |
| 3 | Secondary consumer (carnivore feeding on herbivores) | lizard |
| 4 | Tertiary consumer | hawk |

**Decomposers** (bacteria and fungi) feed on dead remains and faeces at every level and return mineral ions to the soil. A **food web** is a set of interconnected food chains.

**Energy flow.** Energy enters as light, is fixed by producers and flows one way along the chain; it is **not recycled**. At each transfer only about 10 % (usually between 5 % and 20 %) of the energy is passed on. The rest is lost as heat from respiration, in faeces and urine, and in parts that are not eaten (bones, roots, shells). **Efficiency of transfer** = energy in the higher level / energy in the lower level × 100. Because so much is lost, a chain seldom has more than four or five trophic levels.

**Nutrients are recycled, energy is not.** Carbon, nitrogen and other elements pass between organisms and the abiotic environment in cycles.

variantes.quand_utiliser: Questions on pyramids of numbers, biomass or energy, and on inverted pyramids.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
- **Pyramid of numbers**: the number of individuals at each level. It can be **inverted** or spindle-shaped when one large producer supports many consumers (one tree and thousands of insects) or when many small parasites live on one host.
- **Pyramid of biomass**: dry mass of living material per unit area at each level. It is usually upright, but a snapshot of a water body can be inverted because phytoplankton reproduce very fast and are eaten as quickly as they grow.
- **Pyramid of energy**: energy per unit area per year at each level (kJ m⁻² year⁻¹). It is **always upright**, because energy is lost at every transfer.

variantes.nom: Soil as a habitat: abiotic factors
variantes.quand_utiliser: Questions on the distribution of organisms in soil.
variantes.contenu_markdown: The distribution of organisms in soil depends on: **water content** and drainage, **air (oxygen) content**, which depends on particle size and pore space, **pH**, **temperature**, **humus (organic matter) content**, **mineral ion content** and, near the surface, **light**. Soil with a large amount of humus holds water and supports many detritivores such as earthworms; waterlogged soil has little oxygen and few burrowing animals.

variantes.nom: Estimating population size: capture, mark, release, recapture
variantes.contenu_markdown: Capture a sample of n₁ animals, mark them without harming them, release them, then take a second sample of n₂ animals, of which m₂ are marked. The **Lincoln index** is population size N = (n₁ × n₂) / m₂. It assumes that marked animals mix fully with the rest, that marking does not affect survival, and that there is no birth, death or migration between the two samples.

sections.enonce_markdown:
In a grassland ecosystem the energy fixed in the grass is 15 000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹. The energy in the herbivores (primary consumers) is 1 200, in the secondary consumers 150 and in the tertiary consumers 15, all in kJ m⁻² year⁻¹.

(a) Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer between each pair of successive levels. (b) Calculate the percentage of the energy in the grass that reaches the tertiary consumers. (c) State three ways in which energy is lost between grass and herbivores. (d) Explain why there are rarely more than five trophic levels.

etapes.action: Efficiency from producers to primary consumers
etapes.justification: Efficiency = energy in higher level / energy in lower level × 100.

etapes.action: Efficiency at the next two transfers
etapes.justification: Use the same formula for each pair of levels.

etapes.action: Overall percentage reaching the tertiary consumers
etapes.justification: Compare the top level with the first level.
The energy lost is the difference between the two levels.
etapes.resultat_markdown: 15 000 − 1 200 = 13 800 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ is lost: not all the grass is eaten (roots, stems), some eaten material is egested in faeces, and energy is lost as heat in respiration.

etapes.justification: Link the loss at each level to the energy left at the top.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Only 0.1 % of the original energy remains at level 4, which is too little to support another population of carnivores of viable size.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Transfer efficiencies of 8.0 %, 12.5 % and 10.0 % fit the general rule of about 10 %; energy is lost as heat, faeces and uneaten parts, which limits food chains to few levels.

items.erreur_markdown: Energy is recycled between the trophic levels in the same way as carbon.
items.pourquoi_faux: Energy enters as light, is passed along the chain and ends as heat that escapes the ecosystem. Elements such as carbon are recycled; energy is not.
items.correction_markdown: Energy **flows in one direction**; nutrients cycle.

items.erreur_markdown: The arrows in a food chain show which organism is eating which: the hawk arrow points to the lizard.
items.pourquoi_faux: Arrows show the direction of energy flow, from the organism that is eaten to the one that eats it.
items.correction_markdown: Grasshopper → lizard → hawk: each arrow means 'is eaten by'.

items.erreur_markdown: Every pyramid of numbers is an upright pyramid.
items.pourquoi_faux: Numbers depend on body size. One tree can feed thousands of insects, and many parasites live on one host, giving an inverted or spindle shape.
items.correction_markdown: Pyramids of numbers may be inverted; only the pyramid of energy is always upright.

items.erreur_markdown: Only 10 % of energy is lost between trophic levels.
items.pourquoi_faux: The figure is reversed. About 10 % is passed on and about 90 % is lost.
items.correction_markdown: Roughly 10 % is **transferred**; the rest is lost as heat, faeces and uneaten material.

items.enonce_markdown: In a maize field the following feeding relationships occur: maize leaf, grasshopper, lizard, hawk. Decomposers act on the dead remains of each. (a) Write the food chain with arrows. (b) Name the producer and the primary consumer. (c) State the trophic level and the consumer rank of the lizard. (d) What would happen to the grasshopper population if all the lizards were removed, and why?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **maize leaf → grasshopper → lizard → hawk**.

(b) Producer: **maize**; primary consumer: **grasshopper**.

(c) The lizard is at **trophic level 3** and is a **secondary consumer**.

(d) The grasshopper population would at first **increase**, because the predator is gone, until its food supply (maize) or another factor limits it.

items.enonce_markdown: To estimate the number of tilapia in a pond, a student catches 50 fish, marks each with a harmless tag and releases them. The next day 60 fish are caught, of which 12 are tagged. (a) Calculate the estimated population. (b) The pond covers 500 m²; calculate the density in fish per m². (c) State two assumptions of the method. (d) If 15 tagged fish had been found, what estimate would result, and what does the change show?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) N = (n₁ × n₂) / m₂ = (50 × 60) / 12 = **250 fish**.

(b) 250 / 500 = **0.5 fish per m²**.

(c) Marked fish mix completely with the unmarked fish; marking does not affect survival or capture; no immigration, emigration, births or deaths between samples.

(d) N = (50 × 60) / 15 = **200 fish**. A larger fraction of the second sample is marked, which means the population is smaller.

items.enonce_markdown: In an orchard one mango tree (dry mass 600 kg) supports 24 000 caterpillars of mean dry mass 0.05 g each. Six birds of mean dry mass 8 g each feed on the caterpillars. (a) Give the numbers at the three levels and describe the shape of the pyramid of numbers. (b) Calculate the total dry mass of the caterpillars and of the birds, and describe the pyramid of biomass. (c) Calculate the biomass of the caterpillars as a percentage of the tree and the biomass of the birds as a percentage of the caterpillars. (d) Explain why the first percentage is so low.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Numbers 1 : 24 000 : 6. The middle level is the widest, so the pyramid of numbers is **not a pyramid** (it is spindle-shaped), because one large producer supports many small consumers.

(b) Caterpillars: 24 000 × 0.05 = 1 200 g = 1.2 kg. Birds: 6 × 8 = 48 g = 0.048 kg. Biomass 600 kg : 1.2 kg : 0.048 kg gives an **upright pyramid**.

(c) 1.2 / 600 × 100 = **0.2 %**; 48 / 1 200 × 100 = **4.0 %**.

(d) The caterpillars eat only the leaves, not the wood, roots or bark that make up most of the tree's dry mass, and much of what is eaten is lost in respiration and faeces.

items_markdown: An ecosystem is a community plus its abiotic environment; trophic levels run from producers (1) to primary, secondary and tertiary consumers.
Arrows in a food chain show the direction of energy flow, from the eaten to the eater.
Energy flows one way and about 10 % passes to the next level; efficiency = energy in higher level / energy in lower level × 100.
Pyramids of numbers can be inverted or spindle-shaped; pyramids of energy are always upright.
Distribution of organisms in soil depends on water, air, pH, temperature, humus and mineral content.
Population size by capture, mark, release, recapture: N = (n₁ × n₂) / m₂.
